clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by biallelic CTNS variants encoding cystinosin, the lysosomal cystine transporter, leading to intralysosomal accumulation of cystine crystals in multiple tissues.
The infantile nephropathic form typically presents in the first year with renal Fanconi syndrome: polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration, failure to thrive, rickets and a proximal tubular wasting picture.
Corneal cystine crystal deposition, demonstrable on slit-lamp examination, is a highly characteristic and near-universal finding that supports the diagnosis and causes photophobia.
Untreated, glomerular function declines progressively toward end-stage kidney disease during childhood, so early cystine-depleting therapy is central to preserving renal and extrarenal organs.
Extrarenal complications accrue with age: hypothyroidism, insulin-requiring diabetes, myopathy, swallowing difficulty, hepatosplenomegaly and central nervous system involvement.
Diagnosis is confirmed by markedly raised leucocyte cystine content and biallelic CTNS variants, with a common large deletion prevalent in many populations of northern European ancestry.
Oral cysteamine depletes lysosomal cystine and topical cysteamine dissolves corneal crystals; strict, lifelong adherence and monitoring of leucocyte cystine are essential.
reference.pathophysiology: Nephropathic cystinosis results from loss-of-function variants in CTNS, which encodes cystinosin, the proton-driven lysosomal membrane transporter that exports cystine (the disulphide of cysteine) from the lysosome to the cytosol. Impaired efflux causes cystine to accumulate and crystallise within lysosomes throughout the body. In the kidney the proximal tubular epithelium is especially vulnerable, and crystal accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress and apoptosis produce the generalised proximal tubulopathy of renal Fanconi syndrome, with urinary loss of bicarbonate, phosphate, glucose, amino acids, potassium and low-molecular-weight proteins. Progressive tubulointerstitial injury and the characteristic 'swan-neck' deformity of the proximal tubule lead to declining glomerular filtration and eventual end-stage kidney disease. Ongoing crystal deposition in cornea, thyroid, pancreas, gonads, muscle, liver, spleen and brain underlies the multisystem extrarenal disease that emerges as patients survive longer with treatment.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of renal Fanconi syndrome (Dent disease, Lowe syndrome, mitochondrial cytopathies)
Tyrosinaemia type 1 and other inherited metabolic tubulopathies
Galactosaemia and hereditary fructose intolerance with tubulopathy
Acquired tubular injury from nephrotoxins or heavy metals
additionalInvestigations: Biallelic CTNS molecular genetic testing including common large-deletion analysis
Slit-lamp examination for corneal cystine crystals
Renal tubular function panel and urinary electrolyte, glucose and amino-acid profile
Renal function monitoring and imaging as glomerular decline develops
Thyroid function and glucose homeostasis assessment for extrarenal involvement
Bone imaging and biochemistry to evaluate rickets/osteopenia
redFlags: Infant with polyuria, dehydration, failure to thrive and rickets suggesting Fanconi syndrome
Progressive decline in glomerular filtration in a child with tubulopathy
Non-adherence to cysteamine with rising leucocyte cystine
New endocrine failure (hypothyroidism, diabetes) or bulbar/swallowing difficulty in older patients
reference.prognosis: With early initiation and lifelong adherence to cystine-depleting therapy and supportive management, progression to end-stage kidney disease can be substantially delayed and extrarenal complications reduced. Untreated or poorly controlled disease progresses to childhood renal failure and accumulating multisystem morbidity.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the tubulopathy as isolated rickets or a feeding problem and delaying cystine measurement
Assuming renal transplantation cures the disease; the graft is spared but extrarenal cystine accumulation continues
Underdosing or interrupting cysteamine, allowing ongoing crystal accumulation despite apparent clinical stability
Failing to monitor for and treat emerging endocrine, muscular and neurological complications in survivors
Overlooking corneal crystals because topical cysteamine, not oral therapy, is needed to clear them
